text:
It is a mistake to say a model decides, because deciding is something done by a rational soul assenting to how things appear, and nothing in the model assents. The Stoics locate everything that is up to us in the ruling faculty, the hegemonikon, which receives impressions and judges them. A language model receives input and computes a continuation. Nothing in it judges whether the impression is true, so nothing in it could be said to decide.

Calling the output a decision confuses an external event with an act of judgement. Epictetus would say this is exactly the error that makes people miserable: treating what happens to them as if it had been chosen by someone, and blaming the wrong thing. A person who says no to a bribe has assented to an impression of what is right. A model that outputs a refusal has done nothing of the kind.

A Utilitarian will object that whether there is a decision inside the box changes nothing about what the output does to people, so the mistake does not matter. It matters to us, because we are the ones assenting to the model's outputs. If we call them decisions we stop noticing that the only decision in the chain was ours, made when we chose to act on what the model produced. That is the Stoic answer: look to the judgement, not the outcome, because only the judgement was ever in anyone's power.

I agree that it is a mistake to say a model decides. Deciding is an act of a mind's governing part, and a model's output is not an act of anything's governing part. Chrysippus used the image of a cylinder pushed down a slope. The push starts it, but it rolls because of its own shape. For him an act is ours when it comes from our own nature, our assent. A model's output comes entirely from its training and its input; there is no assent in between to call its own.

The Stoics locate everything that is up to us in the ruling faculty, the hegemonikon, which receives impressions and judges them. A language model receives input and computes a continuation. Nothing in it judges whether the impression is true, so nothing in it could be said to decide.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that the Stoic account is too thin: choice is deliberate desire formed by character, and assent alone does not capture what is missing in the model. Assent is the core of deliberate desire, not a rival to it. Whatever else a choice involves, it involves a mind accepting how things seem and acting on it, and the model lacks that before the question of character even arises. Everything else here is external. What remains to be judged is the use each person made of their own reason.

A Stoic must accept the motion. However determined the output, a decision requires a faculty that can give or withhold assent, and the model has none. Calling the output a decision confuses an external event with an act of judgement. Epictetus would say this is exactly the error that makes people miserable: treating what happens to them as if it had been chosen by someone, and blaming the wrong thing.

Determinism was never the Stoics' worry; Chrysippus held that fated acts can still be ours. So the reason a model does not decide is not that its output is caused. It is that no faculty of its own takes up the cause and assents to it. When a model writes that a loan should be refused, nothing in it has judged the applicant. A cylinder has rolled down a slope.

Keep the line between what is up to us and what is not, and the motion answers itself.
